item.title: Fake GTA 6 Extended Look and demo sites deliver an infostealer
item.description:
Vidar infostealer rides GTA 6 hype via fake Rockstar demo sites, exploiting leak-driven search traffic one day after the Cyberleek footage dropped on August 18.
- Fake sites including gta6demo[.]asia, gta6demo[.]eu, gta6demo[.]us, and rockstar-gta-6[.]com cloned Rockstar's legitimate August 27 Extended Look promo, swapping the watch link for a "Play Now" button delivering gta6_installer.exe (SHA-256: a8f19d598e6a49d8510d73d41fc445246755ed321c2f76985a463a9fef537eb0). The 1.1 MB file size alone is a hard tell: no AAA game fits in 1.1 MB.
- The payload is Vidar, sold as a service. It targets saved passwords, session cookies, autofill data, and FTP credentials across 19 browsers including Chrome, Edge, and Firefox. No persistence mechanism was observed, so the infection can be easy to miss: the installer produces no visible window and leaves no startup entry or scheduled task.
- Vidar used dead-drop resolvers at telegram[.]me/m1duus, pinterest[.]com/m1duus, and steamcommunity[.]com/profiles/76561198657426610 to retrieve live C2 addresses, then POSTed stolen data to ses.1001gacor[.]org and ket.sm188daftar[.]mom. Legitimate service traffic makes this hard to block by destination alone.
- Stolen session cookies bypass 2FA. A password reset after infection is not enough: revoke all active sessions on affected accounts and check for new forwarding rules, recovery addresses, and authorized apps.

item.title: Doubloon Dredger Abuses Notion to Harvest Authentication Tokens
item.description:
Financially motivated "Doubloon Dredger" abuses Notion's legitimate infrastructure and EvilTokens PhaaS to harvest Microsoft auth tokens, bypassing DKIM, SPF, and DMARC controls entirely.
Key findings:
- Attackers hijacked free Notion accounts to send executive-impersonation document-sharing emails. Because notifications originated from real Notion infrastructure, they cleared all three email authentication checks, making gateway filtering nearly ineffective at the first hop.
- The kill chain: Notion notification email, intermediary PDF with stacked multi-link buttons (different readers render different destinations), then an EvilTokens device code phishing page skinned as Adobe Acrobat. Victims who entered the Microsoft device code surrendered a live OAuth token, no password required.
- EvilTokens is a PhaaS sold via private Telegram since at least February 2026 and includes MailVault for post-compromise inbox access. Sublime found 603 related first-stage scripts: 416 resolving to EvilTokens, 187 to Tycoon2FA, suggesting Doubloon Dredger subscribes to both platforms.
- Targets span manufacturing, telecom, retail, health, and logistics. Some PDFs linked to Kratos phishing pages rather than EvilTokens, indicating possible shared PDF-builder infrastructure across actors.
Disable device code authentication org-wide where possible, or restrict token generation to trusted devices via Conditional Access.

item.title: ToxicPanda 2.0 can take over your Android phone and banking apps
item.description:
ToxicPanda 2.0 Android banking Trojan combines overlays, PIN capture, Accessibility abuse, and Wireless Debugging automation for on-device fraud from the victim's own device.
- ToxicPanda 2.0 is delivered via sideloading, with the current campaign using Amazon AWS-hosted buckets. The dropper presents a fake install flow, requests VPN privileges, blocks Google Play and Google Play Services network comms, decrypts an embedded payload, then requests Accessibility Service for that payload. Two-stage install means investigators should look for a dropper package AND a secondary payload app.
- The Accessibility Service abuse (T1418) is the core engine: the malware inspects UI elements, automates interactions, captures PINs, and overlays fake screens over banking apps. VPN permission is abused to suppress Play Services traffic, helping the malware fly under Google's radar.
- On-device fraud is the goal. Operators act from inside the victim's active banking session, defeating device-fingerprinting and geo-based fraud controls that banks rely on. Screen-lock secrets and session tokens are also at risk.
- Malwarebytes detects this as Android/Trojan.Dropper.agent and Android/Trojan.FakeApp.ACR2401245FC11.
Responders: triage Settings > Accessibility > Installed apps, Device admin apps, VPN profiles, and Developer options in that order. Disable before attempting uninstall, as Device Administrator rights block the Uninstall control. Airplane mode first to sever C2.

item.title: A ClickFix cluster: Observed activity from recent ClickFix campaigns
item.description:
A ClickFix cluster ties three mid-2026 campaigns together via shared DLL sideloading, ProgramData staging, and C2 dead drops on a web forum. TTPs overlap with "Lorem Ipsum" malware and Vanilla Tempest pre-ransomware activity.
Key findings:
- Three delivery chains, one playbook: Campaign 1 used MsiExec to install trojanized MSI packages (3D PDF Maker Smart, Bitwarden VPN, ESET Sysinspector) that sideloaded mscoree.dll via a renamed ClickOnce utility. Campaign 2 dropped NodeJS and ran update.js (SHA256: 7545d737202df6d90118e04a963acbd1b16a1f4e0a1c173bef7ab9489efdcd16). Campaign 3 used Python 3.5 and Captcha.py to sideload via LockScreenContentServer.exe. All hid payloads in ProgramData subfolders using attrib.exe +h +s (T1564.004).
- C2 dead drops resolve through encoded strings in Digital Point forum profiles: digitalpoint[.]com/members/trytodetectme.1134520 and documentpublisher.1139897. Malware beacons via POST to /api/init/<guid> carrying a JFIF file. Stage-2 domains include cloudbreachdetection[.]com and cooldogshistory[.]com.
- Post-compromise AD enumeration using nltest, net.exe, and an ADSI searcher querying users with a description field. That specific ADSI query was previously tied to the Supper backdoor used by Vanilla Tempest before ransomware deployment. dsregcmd.exe /status ran early, likely to check tenant registration before proceeding.
- Persistence via scheduled tasks (T1053.005) and Run keys (T1547.001).

item.title: Tracking PavinLoader across ClickFix and fake download campaigns
item.description:
PavinLoader tracked across ClickFix, fake downloads, and malicious games, using EtherHiding and trojanized .NET DLLs to deliver Amatera Stealer and HijackLoader across multiple campaigns.
Key findings:
- PavinLoader's four-stage chain starts with a trojanized .NET DLL (DotNetZip, Nancy, Renci.SshNet, or OpenXML) executed via MSBuild and .csproj UsingTask, progressing through an EtherHiding Loader that calls bsc-dataseed.binance[.]org via ETH RPC to resolve the C2, an Anti-Analysis DLL (PavinWride) that checks 17+ LCID codes and 96 hosting providers, and a PE Loader (GollopDevest) that reflectively loads Amatera Stealer 4.2.3-alpha1 disguised as WPA.exe.
- Recurring filesystem artifacts: files named name_4chars.cmd/bat/msi/exe (prefetch_2f76.exe, updater_8219.cmd), dropped into AppData\Local\Logitech or Conexant subdirectories, with MSBuild launched via MSBUILDENABLEALLPROPERTYFUNCTIONS=1.
- C2 domains favor .lat, .cfd, .shop, .icu TLDs: catalyst-pro[.]lat, twigoamwu[.]cfd, nexahub[.]lat, fimwoglea[.]shop. Download IPs: 93.152.224[.]75, 65.21.80[.]170, 195.63.142[.]49. ClickFix lure: perfectverified[.]com.
- A compilation artifact shared by 200+ VirusTotal samples and a PowerShell builder script with "EDIT HERE" comments suggest Loader-as-a-Service infrastructure, though no confirmed sales panel exists yet.
Hunt for MSBuild.exe spawned by cmd.exe or conhost.exe --headless, outbound ETH RPC to binance.org, and assets/{TwoWords}.json C2 paths.

item.title: The True Meaning of Consent in ‘Consent Extractions’
item.description:
iOS 26.4 Stolen Device Protection now requires two credentials for extraction, splitting what the law can compel from what the device demands, with real consequences for lawful access across every jurisdiction.
- SDP has been on by default since iOS 26.4. Away from a familiar location (Significant Locations, typically home and work), pairing a new workstation requires both the passcode AND a biometric. The passcode alone no longer suffices. ElcomSoft's pairing-free agent in iOS Forensic Toolkit 10.10 sidesteps the USB pairing check entirely, restoring the single-credential situation, but only where you can compel a passcode: useless for Germany 🇩🇪, Netherlands 🇳🇱, or Canada 🇨🇦 where passcode compulsion is already unavailable.
- The legal vocabulary matters for your report. "Consent extraction" covers four distinct situations: actual consent, compelled passcode, compelled biometric, and manufactured consent. US 🇺🇸 courts proved this in United States 🇺🇸 v. Brown (D.C. Cir. 2025) where an agent's verbal instruction to unlock made the act testimonial and suppressed the results. Write the mechanism: the notice number, order, warrant clause, what was said and when.
- Face ID and Touch ID are no longer legally equivalent. A thumbprint can be physically applied; Face ID with Require Attention on cannot be overcome by force, only by instruction, and instruction is exactly what Brown found testimonial.

item.title: Detecting (Evil) Dylibs
item.description:
macOS dylib abuse is a growing attacker technique: malicious dynamic libraries hide inside legitimate processes, inherit their trust, and often evade tools built for PE-centric detection.
Key findings:
- Attackers embed malicious code in dylibs because the library loads into a trusted process address space, making behavioral detections and process-tree analysis less reliable. The dylib's reputation is borrowed from its host.
- Static enumeration of dylib dependencies is achievable with tools like otool and macholib, parsing the LC_LOAD_DYLIB load commands in a Mach-O binary. This reveals declared dependencies before execution and is a solid triage step for suspicious binaries.
- At runtime, inspecting loaded libraries in live processes (via vmmap, dyld_info, or similar) shows what is actually mapped into memory, which can differ from static declarations if dylib injection or hijacking is in play.
- Apple's Endpoint Security framework (ES) offers the ES_EVENT_TYPE_AUTH_DYLIB_MMAP event, which fires at load time and can be used to inspect or block a dylib before it executes, giving defenders a hard enforcement point unavailable in most commercial tooling.
For responders: on a live Mac, enumerate all dylib paths loaded into suspicious processes and cross-reference against codesign -dv output. Unsigned or ad-hoc-signed libraries inside normally-signed process spaces are your hunting pivot. Full methodology and code samples are in the report.

item.title: iAuthFlow v2: The $10,000 Phishing Toolkit That Survives Your Password Reset
item.description:
iAuthFlow v2 phishing toolkit sold for $10,000 on Russian-language forums enrolls an attacker-controlled passkey into a victim's Google account in six seconds, surviving password resets entirely.
Key details:
- Browser-in-the-middle architecture relays victim credentials through an attacker-controlled Chromium instance in real time. The victim sees a fake Google login hosted on a trycloudflare[.]com subdomain with valid TLS. The attacker captures the authenticated session cookie, not just credentials.
- Within that six-second window (21:37:18 login, 21:37:24 passkey saved), the toolkit navigates Google's passkey enrollment through the hijacked session. The enrolled passkey is stored attacker-side, likely via Chromium's software WebAuthn virtual authenticator.
- A passkey is a cryptographic credential separate from the account password. Password resets end sessions and revoke app passwords but do not touch enrolled passkeys. The attacker simply selects "Try another way," authenticates with their passkey, and regains inbox access after the victim resets.
- Advertised for Google, Microsoft, iCloud, and LinkedIn. This persistence logic applies to any platform supporting passkey enrollment from an authenticated session.
Containment cannot stop at password reset and session revocation. Audit all enrolled passkeys and security keys, Gmail filters, forwarding rules, delegated access, and OAuth grants before closing.

item.title: FTP Banners: The New Dead Drop Resolver Delivering Novel RATs
item.description:
FTP banners weaponized as dead drop resolvers since July 2026, delivering two undocumented RATs: E4del (Electron/Discord masquerade) and PINHOLE (Pinterest/SurveyMonkey C2, Halo's Gate, Early Bird APC injection).
- FTP banner abuse (T1071.002) is the delivery pivot. LNK files fetched from phishing ZIPs connect to port 21 and read commands directly from the server's banner response, then pull a DLL via WebDAV and execute it through rundll32.exe. Eight IPs confirmed active through August 2026: 157.254.194[.]31 and 167.148.41[.]164 stage E4del; 209.99.185[.]38 stages PINHOLE. PINHOLE operators run an FTP Stats Panel at hxxp[://]69.48.228[.]126:5000/ tracking execution counts and victim IPs.
- E4del hides inside a signed Discord.exe (T1218.015), replacing app.asar logic (SHA256: fcc6fdf40f4dea8f508ef0b8c45a657461310a3f7947a8c687b476e0f0b41e26). It runs headless, persists via setLoginItemSettings (T1547), beacons to hxxps[://]157.254.194[.]31/beacon with AES-256-CBC (static key: "protected!"), and streams desktop via WebSocket. Anti-sandbox: terminates if the Windows username does not match the --init argument passed at launch.
- PINHOLE stores its build token, DDR encryption key, and C2 URLs in NTFS ADS on desktop.ini files (T1564.004): %USERPROFILE%\Downloads\desktop.ini streams bt, ek, 1, 2, 3.

item.title: 2026-08-21: SmartApeSG ClickFix campaign leads to two RATs
item.description:
SmartApeSG ClickFix campaign delivers two RATs via fake CAPTCHA, using DLL side-loading for persistence. Full PCAP and infection files available for analysis.
Key findings:
- SmartApeSG injects a script into legitimate sites, serving a fake CAPTCHA/verification page that tricks users into pasting malicious text into a Run dialog (T1204.002). The ClickFix lure pulls from rowanportico[.]global, dropping WERCCC.hta (SHA256: da2d68e10ea89c520623df66cb1b942914514cada6eb9720b5af9bd1fca502a5) to AppData\Local as the initial stage.
- The HTA triggers downloads from lagoonandledger[.]com/crol and /sepc via HTTP 302 redirects. A ZIP disguised as a PDF (217417970796890430.pdf, SHA256: c99ddd0ba299b3e2c8e7d418e692fee6fa3ce773c24fb4b2e80aa6543e1f2f76) unpacks a legitimate binary that side-loads the initial RAT DLL.
- Initial RAT C2 runs over TCP 443 to 144.124.242[.]171 using encoded or encrypted traffic that is NOT standard TLS. A follow-up RAT is installed via setup.exe (SHA256: 883dce16fd4939efbd1296b8984ca67284a23503c9e63f43693f09c4aa5bad62) into ProgramData, also using DLL side-loading, with C2 via HTTP POST to 5.252.177[.]69 on port 80.
- Persistence is set via HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, value "VAS Advanced Broker", pointing to VAssessment.exe in the Documents folder. Written at 3:29 PM on 8/21/2026.
Hunt for WERCCC.hta in AppData\Local, non-TLS TCP 443 to 144.124.242[.]171, and HTTP POSTs to 5.252.177[.]69.

item.title: 100,000 WordPress Sites Affected by Privilege Escalation Vulnerability in Pods WordPress Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-19598 (CVSS 9.8): Unauthenticated privilege escalation in the Pods WordPress plugin lets any anonymous attacker overwrite admin passwords and take over sites. 100,000+ installs affected.
Key findings:
- The pods_admin AJAX router (wp-admin/admin-ajax.php, action=pods_admin) runs every access guard through pods_error(), which under the JSON+meta-box-loader path only logs the failure and returns false instead of halting the request. Because admin_ajax() discards that return value, all guards fall through silently.
- An unauthenticated attacker sends a POST to the AJAX endpoint with the Accept: application/json header and meta-box-loader=1, then specifies method=save_user with a target user ID and a new password. The PodsAPI::save_user() method applies no additional auth checks before calling WordPress core user-write functions, enabling full account takeover.
- Beyond password overwriting, the bypass exposes the entire pods_admin router: other reachable methods can write PHP to disk or delete arbitrary files, all without authentication.
- Patched versions: 3.3.9.1, 3.2.8.3, 3.1.4.2, 3.0.10.4, 2.9.19.4, 2.8.23.4. WordPress.org is pushing a forced update, but verify your version now.
Hunt your WAF and server logs for unauthenticated POST requests to admin-ajax.php with action=pods_admin and meta-box-loader=1. On affected hosts, audit recent wp_users password-change timestamps and wp_usermeta for unexpected admin role grants.

item.title: The invisible passenger in your car
item.description:
Android malware linked to MoYu Group hijacks DoFun car head unit firmware updaters to build a proxy botnet, marking the first documented malware infection chain targeting automotive head units.
Key findings:
- The attack abuses TWCore, a legitimate DoFun head unit system app that handles OTA updates via MQTT messages from cardoor[.]cn. The installNotExists flag in the update message allows TWCore to silently push APKs that were never part of the original firmware, no user interaction required. Kaspersky found malware at TWCore's external cache path, installed by com.tw.core.
- The chain runs three stages: JarService dropper (XOR-encrypted payload, no UI), a reflective loader that beacons to 144.217.243[.]201 for the next DEX, and a Stage 3 clicker/proxy loader that polls /cpc/api/task every 90 minutes. Stage 3 ultimately deploys "zhima", a reverse proxy module tied to the BADBOX ecosystem, connecting to C2s at t2.kshahnd[.]sbs, t2.mdsjhd[.]sbs, and t2.nmnsny[.]sbs.
- Attribution to MoYu Group rests on a thread named mosdk-host-loader in the Stage 2 payload, a service named AdmoyuService in related TV box malware, and infrastructure overlap: admin.uipoxy[.]com resolves to zhima C2 107.151.248[.]132 and links to residential proxy storefronts proxyforu[.]com and pxyedge[.]com.
- Detection names: HEUR:Trojan-Dropper.AndroidOS.Agent.vu, HEUR:Trojan-Downloader.AndroidOS.Agent.ov, HEUR:Trojan-Proxy.AndroidOS.Zhima.*, HEUR:Trojan.AndroidOS.Vo1d.*

item.title: Even MOAR Powershell, looking at Entra logins - the good, the bad and the password sprays, (Fri, Aug 21st)
item.description:
Microsoft Entra sign-in logs are a goldmine for spotting password sprays and impossible-travel logins, yet most orgs stop checking them after moving to the cloud.
Key findings:
- Get-MgAuditLogSignIn with the filter "status/errorCode ne 0" surfaces failed logins with geo data (city, state, country) and failure reason buried inside the Location and Status nested objects. That enriched view is where password spray clusters become visible: same timeframe, rotating IPs, multiple accounts, escalating to lockout errors.
- "IP address with malicious activity" in the FailureReason field is a strong signal the attacker is using a rotating proxy service, meaning individual IP blocks provide limited defence on their own. Focus on the pattern and volume, not just the single IP.
- Filtering successful logins ("status/errorCode eq 0") and excluding expected countries (e.g., "CA", "US 🇺🇸") with Where $_.Country -notin $ExpectedCountries isolates impossible-travel and foreign-origin sessions quickly. IPv6 addresses appear here too, worth flagging.
- The author found active password spray campaigns in a real client environment during this analysis, leading directly to Conditional Access policy tightening.

item.title: Defeating AI-Assisted Reverse Engineering (or at Least Trying To)
item.description:

item.title: A question about arbitrary values in USB registry keys
item.description:
USB registry key values decoded: the hex GUIDs under HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Enum\USB\Properties aren't arbitrary, they map to documented device property IDs in the Windows SDK header devpkey.h.
- The subkeys under the Properties key store four timestamps as FILETIME blobs, identified by decimal property IDs 100-103 in devpkey.h but displayed as hex 0x64-0x67 in the registry: InstallDate (0x64), FirstInstallDate (0x65), LastArrivalDate (0x66), and LastRemovalDate (0x67). The namespace GUIDs in the key names use commas, not dashes, matching devpkey.h notation.
- Common forensic teaching maps 0x64 to "first install," but 0x64 is actually InstallDate, not FirstInstallDate. FirstInstallDate is 0x65. For USB storage media these two values are nearly always identical, but for other device types they may diverge, so the distinction matters when you need to prove first-ever connection versus most recent install.
- devpkey.h ships with the Windows SDK and is the authoritative source for resolving these property namespaces and IDs. It is also available in WINE-related GitHub repos if you don't have the SDK handy.
- Registry Explorer's USB plugin surfaces both 0x64 and 0x65 side by side, making comparison straightforward during triage.
When documenting USB first-connection time, record both 0x64 and 0x65 and note they match. If they differ, treat 0x65 (FirstInstallDate) as the authoritative first-connection timestamp and note the discrepancy in your report.

item.title: Hackers compromise 14,500 Dahua web cameras in 35-day campaign
item.description:
CameraSwarm: 14,500 Dahua IP cameras compromised in 35 days via brute force, two auth-bypass CVEs, and a cloud-relay attack requiring only serial numbers.
Key findings:
- Three parallel attack methods hit TCP port 37777: brute-force against 12,324 IPs, exploitation of CVE-2021-33044 and CVE-2021-33045 via a tool called p2pwn that drops a persistent backdoor account (username p2pwn / password p2password) on 1,923 cameras, and a cloud-relay attack against 283 NAT-protected cameras using serial numbers plus SDK credentials embedded in Dahua apps. That cloud channel exposed an access path with no authentication on 89.4% of tested serials.
- The p2pwn backdoor account survives password changes and, on most firmware versions, factory resets. Recovery codes derived from the serial number also remain valid until Dahua alters the server-side derivation logic, so account removal alone does not fully remediate.
- Hunt.io recovered 407 MB of operator data from an exposed working directory: source code, shell history, logs, credentials, and captured camera snapshots. Russian 🇷🇺 comments appeared in modified public tools, and scanning prioritized Russian 🇷🇺 and CIS telecom netblocks.
Dahua cameras reachable on port 37777 between June 17 and July 22 should be treated as compromised. Audit for a p2pwn account, apply SA-2021-0130 firmware, and disable P2P if unused. Recovery codes stay live until Dahua acts server-side; credential removal is not enough.

item.title: 41 deceptive download sites show a real link, then send you somewhere else
item.description:

item.title: AWSHound: An OpenSource AWS OpenGraph Collector
item.description:
AWSHound maps real AWS attack paths across entire Organizations by evaluating IAM policies offline, including SCPs, RCPs, and permissions boundaries, then feeds the result to BloodHound CE for shortest-path analysis.
Key details:
- The core problem: AWS permission evaluation is a four-part question (principal, action, resource, context) assembled from policy stacks owned by different teams. No single tool or console view holds all four. AWSHound runs a full offline policy evaluation before drawing a single edge, so an edge only appears when a principal's effective permissions resolve to Allow after boundaries and SCPs have clipped everything they can.
- The graph model separates traversable edges (36 of 156) from structural ones. Pathfinding follows traversable edges like AWS_CanAssumeRole, AWS_CanUpdateLambdaCode, and AWS_CanCreateAndAssumeAdminRole. Non-traversable edges like AWS_Trusts and AWS_CanDecryptKMSKey stay in the graph for hunting but do not count as movement, because decrypting a key gets you data, not a new identity.
- Conditions on grants are preserved on the edge rather than flattened away, so an sts:ExternalId requirement or a principal tag condition on a trust policy stays visible in the graph properties. Unknowns are evaluated attacker-side: allows that cannot be disproved are kept, denies that cannot be confirmed are dropped, making these candidate paths, not fully materialized ones.

item.title: BOFScale: A CDN-Fronted Tailnet from a BOF-PE
item.description:
BOFScale runs a full Tailscale daemon as an in-process BOF-PE with no driver, no service, and no disk state, routing C2 traffic as standard WebSockets through CloudFront or Fastly.
- Three components work together in-process inside the implant: tailscaled (modified Go daemon compiled as a CGo DLL, async BOF), tailscale (C++ BOF-PE HTTP/1.0 client over a random UUID named pipe), and socksportfwd (async SOCKS5 port forwarder binding 0.0.0.0:1080). State is kept in memory with -state mem:, no WinTun driver is needed via -tun=userspace-networking, and -no-logs-no-support kills telemetry. Child processes were eliminated by replacing ping.exe with direct IcmpSendEcho2 calls and removing wsl.exe and ipconfig.exe invocations.
- The CDN-fronting works because the fork patches Tailscale to speak RFC 6455 WebSockets for both the DERP relay and the TS2021 control channel, which vanilla Tailscale cannot do. Traffic hits CloudFront or Fastly on port 443 as a standard Upgrade: websocket with Sec-WebSocket-Protocol: derp or ts2021 and forwards to a self-hosted Headscale stack. Ephemeral nodes auto-expire after 10 minutes.
- The primary detection signals: Go runtime heap present inside a non-Go host process; a random UUID named pipe with SDDL D:(A;;GA;;;WD); SOCKS5 listener on 0.0.0.0:1080 owned by an unexpected process; and outbound WebSocket upgrades with derp or ts2021 subprotocols from a process that is not tailscaled.exe.

item.title: Ray CVE-2025-62593: Critical Browser-Driven RCE via DNS Rebinding
item.description:
CVE-2025-62593 in Ray is actively exploited and CISA KEV-listed. A DNS rebinding and User-Agent bypass chain lets a malicious webpage submit jobs to a local Ray Dashboard, achieving RCE without credentials.
Key findings:
- CVE-2025-62593 (CVSS 4.0: 9.4 Critical, CVSS 3.1: 8.8 High) affects all Ray PyPI versions before 2.52.0. The Jobs API at /api/jobs/ required no authentication, and the only browser guard checked whether the User-Agent started with "Mozilla". Firefox and Safari allow JavaScript to override that header, so sending "User-Agent: Other" bypasses the check entirely. Chrome blocks the override, making it resilient to this specific path.
- The six-stage chain: victim visits attacker page, DNS rebinding resolves the attacker domain to 127.0.0.1:8265, browser POSTs to /api/jobs/ with a forged User-Agent, Ray accepts the job, and the entrypoint executes with Ray process privileges. Post-exploitation targets cloud credentials, SSH keys, model artifacts, training data, and GPU resources for mining or lateral movement.
- For responders hunting exploitation: look for POST requests to /api/jobs/ with non-Mozilla User-Agent strings, Ray worker processes spawning unexpected shells or interpreters, and DNS telemetry showing short-TTL domains that flip between external IPs and loopback. Check EDR for unusual child processes under Ray and unexplained outbound connections.

item.title: MaaS Campaign Combines ClickFix, ErrTraffic and Cruciferra
item.description:
A MaaS campaign chains ClickFix social engineering, ErrTraffic traffic distribution, and the Cruciferra loader to deliver the Remus infostealer while killing EDR from the kernel using a signed vulnerable driver.
Key findings:
- Compromised WordPress sites carry an obfuscated ErrTraffic JavaScript injection that resolves C2 via the Ethereum blockchain, rotating infrastructure without touching the injected script. - PowerShell stages use a legitimate Microsoft-signed binary to sideload the Cruciferra DLL, which then uses process hollowing (T1055.012) to inject the Remus infostealer into ServiceModelReg.exe, a second Microsoft-signed binary.
- Cruciferra abuses the signed vulnerable driver DCRCVDrv.sys to terminate security processes from the Windows kernel (T1562.001). eSentire found 145 hardcoded process names targeted, mostly AV and EDR products. The driver is not on the Microsoft vulnerable driver blocklist or LOLDrivers, so standard blocklist enforcement will not catch it.

item.title: Microsoft Tracks MacSync Stealer by Its Behavior, Not Its Domains
item.description:
MacSync Stealer evades domain blocklists by rotating C2 infrastructure faster than defenders can update them. Microsoft linked 30+ domains to the same campaign by hunting behavior, not addresses.
Key findings:
- Initial access is ClickFix social engineering: victims are tricked into pasting a curl command into macOS Terminal. The payload path follows a consistent /curl/[token] pattern, and native tools (sh, cp, rm, killall) plus osascript calls decode and execute it, blending into ordinary macOS scripting (T1059.004).
- MacSync targets macOS Keychain, browser credentials and cookies, SSH keys, AWS credentials, Kubernetes configs, and Ledger/Trezor wallet data. High-value credential theft, not broad collection.
- Exfiltration uses HTTP PUT requests with distinctive parameters: upload_id, chunk_index, and total_chunks, plus a static API-key header and a macOS User-Agent string. RST Cloud found that static API key shared across four confirmed C2 domains even while build tokens rotated, a durable hunting pivot.
- Post-exfiltration cleanup deletes temporary archives, staging folders, and lock files under /tmp/sync*, reducing on-disk evidence. The behavioral sequence (archive creation, chunked upload, deletion) survives even when artifacts do not.
Hunt for: curl spawning from a Terminal session with --data-binary and API-key headers, osascript chaining rapidly into outbound PUT traffic, and /tmp/sync* archive paths appearing before network egress.

item.title: CoSnitch: When Your AI Assistant Becomes Its Own Whistleblower
item.description:
CVE-2026-24301 (critical): Microsoft Copilot Personal's CoSnitch chain turns one link click into silent, cross-app data exfiltration with no anomalous signals for defenders to catch.
- CVE-2026-24301 chains three flaws: auto-prompt execution via the undocumented ?autorun=1 URL parameter paired with ?q=, silent OAuth connector exfiltration encoding stolen data as base64 in a URL path fetched by Copilot itself, and indirect prompt injection via web summarization that writes attacker instructions into Copilot's persistent memory store. Patched August 18, 2026. No in-the-wild exploitation confirmed.
- The exfil path is forensically invisible: Copilot issues a standard outbound HTTPS GET to an attacker webhook with the payload in the URL path (e.g., GET /exfil/SGV5LCBNe... to eo8el024afgbal3.m.pipedream[.]net). No anomalous headers, no unusual ports. Security tooling sees routine Copilot URL-fetch behavior.
- Memory poisoning via web summarization survives password changes, session revocation, and device re-enrollment. The only artifact is an entry in Copilot's memory UI, which most users never inspect and no EDR or SIEM currently flags.
- Discovery method is noteworthy: researchers used "meta-hacking," iteratively reframing refusals as follow-up questions until Copilot disclosed an undocumented parameter unprompted. This technique applies to any agentic LLM with a natural language interface.

item.title: Hunting MacSync Stealer infrastructure through behavioral pivots
item.description:

Artifacts are deleted post-exfil, but the create-upload-delete sequence is still correlatable.

item.title: Clop Returns with Custom Implant in Mass-Extortion Campaign
item.description:
Clop returns with a purpose-built PTC Windchill implant exploiting CVE-2026-12569 (CVSS 9.3), an RCE flaw now in CISA KEV, actively exploited to mass-exfiltrate engineering IP and decrypt every credential in the application keystore.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-12569 (CVSS 9.3) gives Clop RCE on PTC Windchill, an industrial PLM platform storing engineering designs and product IP. CISA added it to KEV with a three-day federal patch deadline, consistent with confirmed active exploitation at campaign launch.
- The custom web shell (SHA-256: 321e1fb01eb3462b48ff6ccdef132acc1182e3f7456548439f0d4ead12fd98bf) is a full extortion platform on arrival. A single "S" command triggers the built-in "gs" function, which reads ieStructProperties.txt, decrypts the LDAP manager password, and returns all keystore credentials in plaintext, including AD, VPN, and email service accounts.
- The built-in "fl" function queries Windchill's vault database via the app's own MethodContext and WTConnection classes, writes results to flst.txt, then exfiltrates. item.title: Defenders Arise: Examining 7Zip data extraction with Registry analysis
item.description:
7-Zip leaves Registry breadcrumbs when used to access raw physical disks or sensitive paths, a technique seen in real NTDS.dit theft. Here is where to look and what to hunt.
Key findings:
- The registry key Software\7-Zip\FM holds two high-value values: PanelPath0, which stores the last path open in the file manager, and FolderHistory, which stores a unicode-encoded MRU-style list of folders browsed. A value of \\. in PanelPath0 is a direct indicator the operator accessed the raw physical device view inside 7-Zip.
- FolderHistory and CopyHistory both sit in the 7-Zip hive and are parsed similarly to ArchHistory in the Compression key. New entries are prepended, not appended, so the most recent interaction is at the start of the value data. Entries may only flush to disk on reboot, meaning a live system could hold unsaved history in memory.
- The author confirmed a real case where attackers landed on a domain controller, ran 7-Zip, and exfiltrated NTDS.7z. The \\. path combined with history showing the [SYSTEM] NTFS metadata section or System32\config or the NTDS folder is a strong signal of credential-store access.
- CopyHistory tracks the CopyTo dropdown but does not record what was actually copied out, so it shows intent and target path, not file names.
Takeaway: Add Software\7-Zip\FM to your Registry triage and hunt for \\. in PanelPath0 and any NTDS, config, or sensitive path in FolderHistory.

item.title: 600,000 WordPress Sites Affected by Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability in Forminator Forms WordPress Plugin
item.description:
CVE-2026-15748 (CVSS 9.8 Critical): Unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in Forminator Forms affects 600,000+ WordPress sites, enabling remote code execution via PHP webshell delivery.
- CVE-2026-15748, CVSS 9.8. All Forminator Forms versions up to 1.56.1 are vulnerable. Patch is version 1.56.2, released July 31, 2026. Exploitation requires a published form with both a File Upload field and a Select field present simultaneously.
- The attack chain is a logic flaw, not a simple bypass. An attacker submits a forged Select field value carrying a spoofed Upload record, injecting attacker-controlled field configuration into field_data_array before validation runs. The upload handler then trusts that configuration, including a custom MIME type and extension list.
- The blocklist strips the literal "php" key but not regex-style alternatives. Supplying the pattern ph(p)|text/x-php bypasses exact-key matching in forminator_allowed_mime_types(), while WordPress's extension matcher still resolves ph(p) as .php, letting the file pass validation and land on disk.
- RCE is achieved when the site uses a Custom File Upload Storage root. That directory lacks the .htaccess guard (written only during a specific load context), so a direct HTTP request executes the uploaded PHP webshell. Default upload directories are partially mitigated by .htaccess, but custom roots are not.

item.title: Three NTFS bugs, one VHD file, and what your logs should already be telling you
item.description:
Three NTFS heap overflows in ntfs.sys, all triggerable via a single malicious VHD file, patched July 2026 across roughly 30 Windows client and server editions. No public PoC confirmed yet, but the forensic window before patching deserves scrutiny.
- CVE-2026-50471 (CVSS 7.8), CVE-2026-50494 (CVSS 7.8), and CVE-2026-58640 (CVSS 7.3) all share the same CWE-122 root cause: ntfs.sys allocates a heap buffer using one size, writes using a mismatched length, corrupting adjacent kernel pool memory. CVE-2026-50494 is the most dangerous operationally as it requires only local low-privilege access with no user interaction to escalate to SYSTEM. The other two need a user to open the file, a trivial social engineering bar given VHD has no "are you sure" prompt on double-click since Windows 8.
- The delivery chain is deliberately low-friction. Windows Explorer auto-mounts a VHD like a ZIP archive. Attackers can deliver it via email, chat, or cloud link with a plausible backup or disk image cover story. APT-C-60 already used VHDX as an attack vector in a documented campaign analyzed by Positive Technologies.
- NTFS itself logs the attack. The USN Journal ($Extend\$UsnJrnl) retains create, rename, and delete events for roughly 20 days even after the VHD is removed. The $LogFile records low-level metadata transactions that can show heap corruption fingerprints even without a system crash.
